title: The Empty Flower Patch
learning_objectives: Use evidence from the story to explain a choice.
parent_prompts: Before reading: What do you notice in the title?
After reading: What helped the characters decide?

pages.text: On the first warm morning of spring, Iva found the school garden strangely quiet. The yellow flowers were open, yet the familiar hum around them seemed faint. She wrote down what she noticed instead of announcing that the bees had vanished.
pages.audio_script: On the first warm morning of spring, Iva found the school garden strangely quiet. The yellow flowers were open, yet the familiar hum around them seemed faint. She wrote down what she noticed instead of announcing that the bees had vanished.
pages.image_alt: Iva observes a quiet school flower patch in the morning.

pages.text: Her classmates offered explanations immediately. One blamed a new path beside the garden; another pointed to the cloudy sky. Their teacher asked which ideas could be checked and which were only guesses. Iva drew a chart with separate spaces for observations and possible causes.

pages.image_alt: Classmates discuss several ideas beside the school garden.

pages.text: The children watched the same flower patch at three different times. Morning was quiet, but several bees appeared when the sun warmed the stones. The pattern challenged the claim that the insects had disappeared completely, although it did not explain every difference.

pages.image_alt: Bees visit the flower patch when the sun warms the garden.

pages.text: They compared the yellow patch with a second bed near the library. That bed had more open flowers and more visitors during their short watches. Iva reminded the group that a difference between beds was a clue, not proof that flower color alone caused it.

pages.image_alt: Children compare two flower beds with different numbers of blooms.

pages.text: At the garden shed, the caretaker showed them a watering schedule and explained that some plants had bloomed later than expected. The class checked their own sketches from the previous week. They found fewer open flowers then, but their notes were too brief for a confident comparison.

pages.image_alt: Iva checks old garden sketches and a caretaker's watering notes.

pages.text: A friend proposed planting many new flowers at once. Iva liked the idea but asked what would happen if the seedlings needed more water than the garden could spare. Together, they chose a small trial bed and agreed to watch it before making a larger change.

pages.image_alt: The class prepares a small trial flower bed rather than changing the whole garden.

pages.text: The class selected plants already growing well in nearby gardens and asked the caretaker where a new bed would be safe. They also left an undisturbed corner with leaves and stems. Their plan addressed several possible needs without pretending they had identified one certain cause.

Their plan addressed several possible needs without pretending they had identified one certain cause.
pages.image_alt: The class chooses a safe spot for plants and leaves one corner undisturbed.

pages.text: For four weeks, pairs of students counted open flowers and visiting insects during the same short afternoon window. Rain interrupted one count, so they marked it as missing rather than filling in a number they had not observed. Their chart slowly became more useful.

pages.image_alt: Children record insect visits in a notebook while rain interrupts a garden watch.

pages.text: The trial bed flowered, and the children saw more insect visits there on some afternoons. Other afternoons remained quiet. Iva reported both results at the school meeting, explaining that weather, timing, and the number of open flowers could all affect what a short observation showed.

pages.text: The principal asked whether the school should replace every lawn with flowers. Iva answered that the trial supported adding another small bed, not changing the entire grounds immediately. The caretaker agreed to help, provided the class could maintain the new plants through dry weeks.

pages.text: By the end of term, the garden held more flowers and a better record of what the children had seen. Iva still could not say exactly why that first morning had been quiet. She could say something more valuable: they had learned to care without claiming certainty they did not have.

quiz.prompt: What did the morning observation actually show?

options.text: The patch was quiet at that time
The new path caused the quiet

quiz.explanation: Page 1 reports a quiet patch, not a proven cause.

quiz.prompt: Why do the students mark a rainy count as missing?

options.text: They did not observe a reliable number
They wanted the chart to look neat

quiz.explanation: Page 8 says rain interrupted the count, so they did not invent a number.

quiz.prompt: Why does Iva support only another small bed?

options.text: The trial supports a limited next step
The garden has no other space

items.text: On the first warm morning of spring, Iva found the school garden strangely quiet. The yellow flowers were open, yet the familiar hum around them seemed faint. She wrote down what she noticed instead of announcing that the bees had vanished.

At the garden shed, the caretaker showed them a watering schedule and explained that some plants had bloomed later than expected. The class checked their own sketches from the previous week. They found fewer open flowers then, but their notes were too brief for a confident comparison.

By the end of term, the garden held more flowers and a better record of what the children had seen. Iva still could not say exactly why that first morning had been quiet. She could say something more valuable: they had learned to care without claiming certainty they did not have.
